To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the role of governments and other relevant actors in the development of adaptive capacities of agriculture and coastal territories is crucial, that the development of adaptive capacity is a complex process that requires an understanding of the roles of all relevant actors, and that the development of pertinent adaptive capacity requires a co-construction approach.

the roles of actors are not as important as the adaptive capacity that they have to develop, and the adaptive capacity is the result of the interplay of the roles of actors and the context within which they operate.

(a) governments are important in the battle against CCV but not in the ways that we have traditionally thought; (b) the role of governments is more complex and more nuanced and includes the role of supporting other actors and their adaptive capacities; and (c) the roles of governments are more important in developing countries than in developed countries, where the role of other actors, particularly collective actors, is more important.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to increase the adaptive capacity of these actors to CCV and to reduce the negative impacts of CCV.
the development and use of a new theoretical and conceptual framework for understanding the roles of governments, other institutions and individual actors in the process of adaptation to CCV.

understanding how different actors can develop and increase their adaptive capacities to CCV, particularly in developing countries where they are often the most vulnerable to the negative impacts of this phenomenon.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no conclusive statements to be found, but there are many lessons learned and some important conclusions to be drawn from this research that can help to guide future action and research.
governments and their institutions are not the only actors involved in the adaptation process.
there is no one-size-fits-all model to address the CCV challenge, but rather that there are a multitude of models that are all important and that need to be considered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the role of governments is not the most important in adaptation to CCV, although it is an important one, and that the role of other actors, including collective and individual citizens, is much more important and is a critical component of the adaptation process.
governments have important but not necessarily the most important roles to play, but that they can play them in a variety of different ways.
governments need to develop the adaptive capacities of their actors, and not only the adaptive capacities of themselves as governments.
The main takeaway from our work is that

governments and other actors need to be more involved in the development of adaptive capacity of all types of actors in order to increase the effectiveness of their actions in dealing with the challenges that CCV presents.
the development of pertinent adaptive capacities is a co-construction of all the actors involved and that this is a process that needs to be facilitated by governments.
governments and other actors have important roles to fulfill, but the way they do so is not always obvious, and it is important to understand the different ways in which they can do this.
